title: Textbook companion: trace the systemic arteries
summary: Textbook sections 21.4–21.5: route tracing supplements the lecture physiology.
objectives: Relate vessel names to body regions
takeaways: Trace the entire route instead of memorizing isolated names.
Distinguish arterial supply from venous drainage.

steps.title: Aorta and arch branches
steps.text:
Blood leaves the left ventricle through the ascending aorta, aortic arch and descending aorta. The coronary arteries arise near the aortic root to supply myocardium.

The arch branches are the brachiocephalic trunk, left common carotid and left subclavian arteries. The brachiocephalic trunk divides into the right common carotid and right subclavian. This right-left asymmetry adds one named segment to the route toward the right arm.

check.q: Which arch branch supplies the right carotid and right subclavian?

steps.title: Two arterial approaches to the brain
steps.text:
Common carotid arteries divide into external carotids for much of the face and scalp and internal carotids for the cranial circulation. Vertebral arteries arise from subclavians and ascend to join as the basilar artery.

The internal-carotid and vertebrobasilar systems communicate through the cerebral arterial circle. Follow the route rather than assuming the common carotid enters the skull unchanged.

check.q: Where do vertebral arteries originate and what do they form?
check.a: They arise from the subclavian arteries and unite to form the basilar artery.

steps.title: From the shoulder to the fingers
steps.text:
Subclavian becomes axillary, then brachial as it passes regional boundaries. The brachial divides into radial and ulnar arteries. Palmar arches distribute blood into digital branches.

The radial contribution predominates in the deep palmar arch and the ulnar contribution in the superficial arch. The arches anastomose, so these are connected routes, not two completely isolated hand circulations.

check.q: Trace a direct route from the left subclavian to the radial artery.
check.a: Left subclavian → axillary → brachial → radial artery.

steps.title: Thoracic and abdominal branches
steps.text:
The descending thoracic aorta supplies thoracic organs and walls. Below the diaphragm, the abdominal aorta gives paired branches to organs such as the kidneys and unpaired digestive branches.

The celiac trunk supplies foregut-associated organs including stomach, liver and spleen. Superior and inferior mesenteric arteries supply successive intestinal territories. Distinguish arterial supply from portal venous drainage: these are different routes through the same organ region.

check.q: Which three major unpaired abdominal branches supply digestive territories?
check.a: Celiac trunk, superior mesenteric artery and inferior mesenteric artery.

steps.title: Pelvis, thigh, leg and foot
steps.text:
The abdominal aorta divides into common iliac arteries. Internal iliacs supply pelvic territories; external iliacs continue as femoral arteries in the thigh and popliteal arteries behind the knee.

The popliteal branches into anterior and posterior tibial routes. The posterior tibial gives a fibular branch and plantar branches; the anterior tibial continues toward dorsalis pedis. Follow each named region to keep the sequence straight.

check.q: Trace the route from common iliac artery to popliteal artery.
check.a: Common iliac → external iliac → femoral → popliteal.

practice.q: Order the arterial route to the right forearm.
Order the arterial route to the knee.
The vertebral arteries join to form the…
practice.why: The vertebral arteries join intracranially as the basilar artery.

practice.q: The celiac trunk supplies which group?
Name the three aortic arch branches.
practice.a: Brachiocephalic trunk, left common carotid and left subclavian arteries.

practice.q: Why is the right upper-limb route one branch longer from the arch?
practice.a: It passes through the brachiocephalic trunk before the right subclavian.

title: Textbook companion: trace systemic venous return
summary: Textbook sections 21.4–21.5: route tracing supplements the lecture physiology.
objectives: Relate vessel names to body regions
takeaways: Trace the entire route instead of memorizing isolated names.
Distinguish arterial supply from venous drainage.

steps.title: Three main returns to the right atrium
steps.text:
The superior vena cava receives the upper body, the inferior vena cava the lower body, and the coronary sinus much of the heart wall’s venous return. Some cardiac veins enter the right atrium directly.

Deep veins often accompany arteries; superficial veins run in subcutaneous tissue. Dural venous sinuses are channels associated with the cranial dura. Venous routes are not always identical to arterial routes in reverse.

check.q: Name the three principal venous entries to the right atrium.
check.a: Superior vena cava, inferior vena cava and coronary sinus.

steps.title: Head, neck and upper limb
steps.text:
Dural sinuses drain toward the internal jugular veins. Each internal jugular joins the subclavian to form a brachiocephalic vein; the two brachiocephalics join the SVC.

Deep arm return passes through radial/ulnar, brachial and axillary veins. Superficial cephalic and basilic pathways connect with deep return; the median cubital commonly links them near the elbow. Axillary becomes subclavian.

check.q: Trace a route from internal jugular to right atrium.
check.a: Internal jugular → brachiocephalic → superior vena cava → right atrium.

steps.title: Thoracic return and the azygos system
steps.text:
The azygos system collects much of the thoracic wall’s venous return. Left-sided hemiazygos and accessory hemiazygos channels connect with the azygos vein, which drains into the SVC.

Ascending lumbar connections provide continuity with abdominal wall drainage. These channels show why the venae cavae are connected by collateral routes rather than being isolated pipes.

check.q: Where does the azygos vein ultimately drain?

steps.title: Lower-limb superficial and deep paths
steps.text:
Deep return from tibial and fibular veins reaches popliteal, femoral, external iliac and common iliac veins, then the IVC. The great saphenous joins the femoral vein; the small saphenous usually joins the popliteal.

Venous valves and skeletal-muscle compression promote return against gravity. Superficial and deep routes communicate, but a named superficial vein should not be substituted for an artery with a similar location.

check.q: Which deep veins receive the great and small saphenous veins?
check.a: Great saphenous → femoral; small saphenous → popliteal, in the usual arrangement.

steps.title: The portal detour through the liver
steps.text:
Most venous blood from the digestive tract reaches the liver through the hepatic portal vein. It crosses hepatic sinusoids before hepatic veins return it to the IVC. Thus two capillary beds occur in series before blood returns to the heart.

The liver also receives arterial blood. The portal vein delivers nutrient-rich venous blood; the hepatic veins drain the liver. Confusing portal inflow with hepatic outflow reverses the mechanism.

check.q: Trace venous blood from small intestine to IVC through the portal route.
check.a: Intestinal veins → superior mesenteric vein → hepatic portal vein → hepatic sinusoids → hepatic veins → IVC.

practice.q: Order venous return from the brain.
Order deep return from the knee.
The great saphenous typically joins the…
practice.why: It joins deep return through the femoral vein.

practice.q: Which carries blood away from hepatic sinusoids toward the IVC?
What is special about the hepatic portal route?
practice.a: Blood crosses digestive capillaries then hepatic sinusoids before returning to the heart.

practice.q: Which large thoracic vein receives azygos blood?
